# Non-Programmers Can Label Programs Indirectly via Active Examples: A Case Study with Text-to-SQL

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#apel)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.312.pdf) · EMNLP 2023 proceedings, pp. 5126–5152

**Reading coverage:** All 27 pages including main sections 1–8, limitations and Appendices A–M: Bayesian derivation, proposed extensions, synthesis constraints, schema fixes, candidate generation, error/cost studies, complete annotator tutorial and regex experiment. Interface figures 11–12 visually inspected.

## Research question

Non-programmers cannot readily inspect complex SQL, yet reliable annotation and intent verification require distinguishing subtly different programs.

## Method

APEL maintains a prior over candidate SQL equivalence classes, synthesizes small databases that maximize expected information gain, and asks annotators to choose the intended output. Bayesian updates and a learned annotator-error model combine noisy responses. A fuzz-then-drop heuristic trades informativeness against database size.

## Evaluation

An oracle simulation and a study with 11 university non-programmers evaluate Spider-derived tasks. The human study covers 240 utterances, approximately 2.5 annotators per utterance and up to three questions per annotator. Two authors establish corrected reference annotations using APEL-assisted adjudication; candidate matching uses randomized test suites.

## What the results support

On the corrected human-study reference, APEL reaches 75% annotation accuracy versus the seed parser’s 59%, matching the original Spider labels’ 75%. The candidate ceiling is 88%. Interaction exposes schema misunderstandings, missing zero-count entities and tie-handling errors.

## Limits and qualifications

The result is annotation accuracy, not demonstrated downstream parser training or proven cost superiority over experts. The reference was created with the evaluated framework, and finite random testing only approximates SQL equivalence. Candidate coverage, unnatural synthetic databases, arithmetic burden and vague utterances limit reliability. Explicit unanswerable labeling is not supported.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

A substantive human-tested approach to clarification through concrete counterexamples and to auditing benchmark semantics, especially when natural-language paraphrases hide program differences.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| APEL demonstrates cheaper expert-equivalent labeling and better trained parsers. | The study reports matched annotation accuracy but explicitly states that neither downstream fine-tuning benefit nor comparative annotation cost was empirically validated. | §6.5, Table 2; Limitations p. 5135; Appendix A | Limit conclusion to measured annotation accuracy. |
| APEL handles unanswerable requests. | The orchestra/company founding example requires an insufficient-information label, but §6.6 states that neither Spider nor APEL supports that option. | §6.6, p. 5132 | Distinguish identification in qualitative feedback from supported output behavior. |
| Candidate equivalence is formally proven. | Candidates are merged by matching results on 1,000 random databases; exact equivalence is available only for the separate regex experiment. | §4.2; Appendix M | Describe SQL equivalence as approximate test-suite agreement. |
